name: 5:2 diet

lead: The 5:2 diet has people eat normally five days a week and limit intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days. People use it as a flexible way to lose fat and get leaner.

The two low days create a weekly calorie deficit, and the fat lost changes how the face and body look. It was popularised in 2012 after a BBC documentary, and trials and meta-analyses report weight loss comparable to continuous calorie restriction, in people with obesity and fatty liver disease among others.

paras: People pick two non-consecutive days, such as Monday and Thursday, for the low-calorie meals and eat as usual on the others. Many find it easier to stick to than daily dieting because most days are unrestricted. Results build over weeks to months.
Hunger, irritability and headaches are reported early on. It is not recommended in pregnancy, for young people, older adults, underweight people or anyone with an eating-disorder history.

angle.text: People use the 5:2 pattern as a flexible way to build a weekly calorie deficit, lose fat and look leaner. Studies show weight loss similar to standard dieting.

lead: The 5:2 diet is an intermittent fasting pattern in which people eat normally for five days a week and limit intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days.[1] It was popularised in the UK and Australia by Michael Mosley after a 2012 BBC documentary.[1]
It is used for weight loss and leanness. Randomized trials have compared it with continuous calorie restriction and with other diets, in people with obesity and with fatty liver disease.[2][3][4]
Reviews report weight loss similar to other calorie-restriction approaches; its long-term effects remain little studied.[1][5]
infobox: 5 normal days, 2 restricted days per week

paras: The 5:2 diet is one of the main forms of intermittent fasting, alongside alternate-day fasting and time-restricted eating.[1][6] The approach was first documented in a 2011 study co-authored by Michelle Harvie and Mark Mattson and drew public attention through the 2012 BBC2 Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer.[1]

A 2023 meta-analysis compared alternate-day fasting, the 5:2 diet and time-restricted eating for weight loss.[7] An umbrella review of meta-analyses graded the evidence for intermittent fasting on obesity-related outcomes.[5] Wikipedia summarises weight loss in most human studies as about 2.5 to 9.9 percent, mostly fat, with limited evidence of an advantage over continuous calorie restriction.[1]

Reported early effects include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, usually fading within about a month.[1] The diet is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people, and people with or at risk of eating disorders; the US National Institute on Aging does not recommend it for the general public.[1]
A 50-week randomized trial tested intermittent calorie restriction in the form of the 5:2 diet against continuous calorie restriction for body weight and metabolism.[3]
A 12-week randomized trial in 74 people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease compared the 5:2 diet with a low-carbohydrate high-fat diet on liver fat.[4]
A pilot study examined two days of energy restriction per week in obese men.[8]

A randomized trial examined whether metabolic improvements under calorie restriction depended on gut microbiome composition, and a meta-analysis examined intermittent fasting in fatty liver disease.[9][10]

timeline.event: Study co-authored by Harvie and Mattson documents the approach.[1]
